title: Super El Nino, below-normal monsoon: How Keralam is bracing for weather extremes
content: This year's El Nino event, tagged by many as 'Super El Nino' and which has been underway since June, has already broken a number of records. It has even reshaped the world's weather, causing fires in Indonesia and triggering typhoons in the west Pacific. Climate scientists have put the temperature in the core part of tropical Pacific where the El Nino is monitored as 3.5 degrees Celsius above normal in September and may reach 4 degrees during November-December. Besides, this is further expected to break many more records in world temperatures. El Nino, a natural climate phenomenon in which the surface waters of the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, thereby changing atmospheric circulation and influencing weather patterns across the world, including India's monsoon, is feared to cause unprecedented extreme weather exigencies in the months to come. Coupled with a below average South West Monsoon that went past and the unpredictable North-east monsoon that is underway Keralam is expected to brace for as many severe flooding as draught conditions. However, on July 30 this year, the PIB posted on its website a statement by the Ministry of Earth Sciences under the rubric 'Parliament Question: Impact Of El Nino On Indian Monsoon', that "There is no officially defined category known as a 'Super El Nino' by the World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) or the India Meteorological Department (IMD), under the Ministry. Operationally, El Nino events are generally classified as weak, moderate, strong, or very strong based on the magnitude of sea surface temperature anomalies over the equatorial central Pacific Ocean." Though this may somewhat assuage fear of the periodic climatic phenomenon, researchers and weather analysts are predicting a situation which may raise severe concerns. According to Neetha K Gopal, who is presently heading the Meteorological Centre of IMD in Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam experienced below-normal monsoon rains in the past months. "The low rains and the rise in temperature are triggered by the presence of El Nino in the Pacific. There has been an extreme shortage of rain during the South-West monsoon season from June to September." Meanwhile, a similar trend is expected for the North East monsoon that spans between October and December as well. "The El Nino condition is expected to continue till late February, and this could also impact the summer season in the year ahead and could trigger heat wave conditions like those in the previous El Nino years like 2015-16 and 2023-24," she told Onmanorama. Climate experts say the ongoing El Nino is likely to peak at the end of 2026 and push average global temperatures to record levels next year. Severe climate events like heat waves, flash floods, landslides, cloudbursts and so on are possible eventualities that may throw normal life out of gear. Meanwhile, Shekhar Lukose Kuriakose, Member Secretary, Kerala State Disaster Management Authority (KSDMA), shared several questions and concerns regarding weather extremes and climate eventualities. The importance of flood mitigation and town master plans El Nino is literally a climatic phenomenon like any other. In Keralam, the more impact it unleashes is drought and heat, which triggers preparation for water scarcity after December. The general practice is that after assessing the kharif season, which extends from June to October, the government agency decides to declare whether a place is drought-hit or not. Similarly, the rabi crop season that ensues is assessed, and the State Relief Commissioner (KSDMA) decides on the quantum of compensation and relief measures. But, preparing for pluvial flooding (urban flooding) is not something that we should be doing just for El Nino or La Nina (Caused by unusually cold sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean) or cyclonic storms. It should be an integral part of urban planning...
